facts.statement: An immediate annuity is bought with a single payment, and income typically starts within one year.
facts.quote: With an immediate annuity, you make a single payment to purchase the annuity and typically start receiving income payments within one year of purchase.

items.stem: At age 70, Dana buys an annuity with one lump-sum payment, and her monthly income checks begin a few weeks later. Dana bought:
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, an immediate annuity is bought with a single payment and income typically begins within one year of purchase.

facts.statement: In a deferred annuity, the period when money grows before income begins is the accumulation phase.
facts.quote: This time period during which your money is allowed to grow is called the accumulation phase.

items.stem: In a deferred annuity, what is the period before income payments begin called?
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, the period during which the money is allowed to grow is the accumulation phase. Income payments begin in the payout phase.
items.retired: Flagged as test-wise in two rounds: the payout-phase synonyms make the key the odd one out. The accumulation and payout phases are covered by I4-01a and I4-06a context.

facts.statement: A fixed annuity guarantees at least a minimum interest rate during accumulation; only the minimum is guaranteed.
facts.quote: Fixed annuities guarantee your money will earn at least a minimum interest rate during the accumulation phase.

items.stem: During the accumulation phase, what does a fixed deferred annuity guarantee?
options: Its current interest rate for the life of the contract
Returns tied to a stock index
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, fixed annuities guarantee at least a minimum interest rate. They may credit more, but only the minimum is guaranteed.

facts.statement: A fixed indexed annuity's credited interest is guaranteed never to be less than zero, even if the market goes down.
facts.quote: The interest rate is guaranteed to never be less than zero, even if the market goes down.

items.stem: The benchmark index for Ray's fixed indexed annuity falls 12% during a one-year term. The interest credited to his annuity for that term is:
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, a fixed indexed annuity's credited interest is guaranteed never to be less than zero, even if the market goes down. Negative crediting limited by a buffer describes a RILA.
items.retired: Ambiguous against common exam-prep teaching that indexed annuities guarantee a minimum rate; the floor concept is covered by I4-05a's contrast with RILAs.

facts.statement: Unlike a fixed indexed annuity, a registered index-linked annuity (RILA) can lose money when the index performs poorly.
facts.quote: However, unlike a fixed index annuity, you can lose money in a RILA.

items.stem: Which type of deferred annuity can credit negative interest, reducing contract value, when its benchmark index performs poorly?
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, a RILA can credit negative interest when the index performs poorly, so the owner can lose money. A fixed indexed annuity's credited interest never falls below zero.

facts.statement: A variable annuity lets the owner direct contributions among mutual funds, with no limits on gains or losses.
facts.quote: Variable annuities allow you, during the accumulation phase, to direct your contributions to a menu of different mutual funds. There are no limitations on losses or gains

items.stem: Which type of annuity lets the owner direct contributions among a menu of mutual funds, with no limit on gains or losses?
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, variable annuities let the owner direct contributions to a menu of mutual funds, with no limits on losses or gains.

facts.statement: Of the four main deferred annuity types, RILAs and variable annuities are securities that must register with the SEC.
facts.quote: Of the four main types of deferred annuities shown above, RILAs and variable annuities are securities that must register with the SEC.

items.stem: Of the four main types of deferred annuities, which two are securities that must register with the SEC?
options: Fixed annuities and fixed indexed annuities
Fixed indexed annuities and variable annuities
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, RILAs and variable annuities are securities that must register with the SEC. Fixed and fixed indexed annuities are insurance products regulated by the states.

facts.statement: In a registered MVA annuity, the insurer pays a fixed rate for a period but may adjust contract value, often down, on early withdrawal.
facts.quote: In a registered MVA annuity, the insurer pays a fixed rate of interest over a specified period, but may adjust the value of your contract, often down, if you withdraw money early.

items.stem: An owner of a registered MVA annuity withdraws money before the end of the specified interest period. What can the insurer do?
options: Change the contract's value, often reducing it
Pay a higher fixed rate for the rest of the period
Convert the contract into an index-linked annuity
Waive any charges, since the rate was fixed
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, a registered MVA annuity pays a fixed rate over a specified period but may adjust the contract value, often down, if money is withdrawn early.

facts.statement: An insurer's obligations under an annuity depend on its financial strength and claims-paying ability.
facts.quote: an insurance company’s obligations under an annuity contract are subject to its financial strength and claims-paying ability

items.stem: The guarantees in an annuity contract are backed primarily by:
options: The performance of a stock index
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, an insurer's obligations under an annuity are subject to its financial strength and claims-paying ability. Annuities are not FDIC-insured.

facts.statement: Annuities provide tax-deferred growth until income payments begin.
facts.quote: Annuities provide: tax-deferred growth until you begin receiving income payments

items.stem: Which feature do annuities generally provide before income payments begin?
options: FDIC insurance on the account value
A guaranteed return above market rates
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, annuities provide tax-deferred growth until income payments begin.

facts.statement: Withdrawing an annuity's value as a lump sum may bring surrender charges, taxes and tax penalties.
facts.quote: you may choose to withdraw your contract’s value as a lump sum payment, although doing so may subject you to surrender charges, taxes, and tax penalties

items.stem: Early in the contract, an annuity owner withdraws the full contract value as a lump sum. Which costs may apply?
options: A flat processing fee, with income tax deferred to age 65
Surrender charges, plus income tax on gains and possible penalties
Income tax on the full amount, with surrender charges waived
A market value adjustment in every case, but no tax
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, withdrawing an annuity's value as a lump sum may bring surrender charges, taxes and tax penalties.
items.retired: Flagged as test-wise in two rounds: the complete, hedged key stands out against absolute distractors.

facts.statement: For a RILA, the insurer generally sets parameters that limit both gains and losses.
facts.quote: The insurer generally sets parameters that limit both your gains and your losses.

items.stem: In a registered index-linked annuity (RILA), the insurer generally sets parameters that:
options: Limit gains but guarantee no losses
Limit losses but allow unlimited gains
Lock in a minimum fixed interest rate
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, the insurer generally sets RILA parameters that limit both gains and losses.

facts.statement: A participation rate credits only a percentage of the index gain.
facts.quote: if the participation rate is 75% and the index return is calculated to be 10% during the measuring period, the return credited to your annuity would be 7.5%

items.stem: An indexed annuity has an 80% participation rate and no cap or spread. The index gains 10% over the measuring period. What is credited?
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor Bulletin: Indexed Annuities, the participation rate sets how much of the index gain is credited. Eighty percent of 10% is 8%.

facts.statement: A rate cap is the maximum positive return the contract can earn in a period.
facts.quote: The rate cap is a maximum rate of positive return that your contract can earn.

items.stem: A client's indexed annuity carries a 6% rate cap. The linked index rises 11% this crediting period, and there is no participation limit or spread. What is credited?
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor Bulletin: Indexed Annuities, a rate cap is the maximum positive return the contract can earn, so an 11% index gain is credited at the 6% cap.

facts.statement: A spread (margin or asset fee) subtracts a set percentage from the index gain.
facts.quote: This fee subtracts a set percentage from any gain in the index.

items.stem: An indexed annuity has a 2.5% spread and no cap or participation limit. The index gains 8%. What is credited?
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor Bulletin: Indexed Annuities, a spread subtracts a set percentage from any gain in the index: 8% minus 2.5% is 5.5%.

facts.statement: When features combine, the participation rate is applied first and then the spread is subtracted.

items.stem: An indexed annuity has a 50% participation rate and a 1% spread. The participation rate is applied to the index gain first, and then the spread is subtracted. The index gains 12%. What is credited?
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor Bulletin: Indexed Annuities, combined features are applied in sequence: 12% times 50% is 6%, minus the 1% spread is 5%.

facts.statement: Index gains are usually calculated without dividends paid on the index's securities.
facts.quote: Any gains in the value of the index are generally calculated without including dividends paid on the securities that make up the index.

items.stem: An index reports a 9% total return for the year, of which 2% came from dividends. Under a typical indexed annuity, the index gain used to calculate the credit is:
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor Bulletin: Indexed Annuities, index gains are generally calculated without dividends, so 9% minus 2% of dividends leaves 7% before any participation rate, cap or spread.

facts.statement: A floor limits loss to a set percentage; a buffer (shield) absorbs a set percentage of loss before the owner loses value.
facts.quote: Buffer or Shield. This protection offers a set percentage of loss that the insurance company is willing to absorb before deducting value from the indexed annuity.

items.stem: An index-linked annuity has a 10% buffer. The index falls 15% in the period. Before any surrender charges, how much does the contract value lose?
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor Bulletin: Indexed Annuities, a buffer absorbs a set percentage of loss first. A 15% drop minus the 10% buffer leaves a 5% loss. A 10% floor would instead cap the loss at 10%.

facts.statement: With a floor, the owner's loss stops at the floor percentage.
facts.quote: This protection limits investor exposure to a set percentage of potential loss.

items.stem: Which index-linked annuity feature caps the owner's loss at a set maximum percentage, with the insurer absorbing any decline beyond that point?
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor Bulletin: Indexed Annuities, a floor limits exposure to a set percentage of potential loss. A buffer instead absorbs the first set percentage of loss, and the owner bears the rest.

facts.statement: Under the point-to-point method, the index level is compared at two points in time, such as the start and end of the period.
facts.quote: This method compares the index level at two points in time, such as the beginning and ending dates of the time period.

items.stem: Which indexing method compares the index level only at the beginning and end of the crediting period?
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor Bulletin: Indexed Annuities, the point-to-point method compares the index level at two points in time, such as the beginning and ending dates of the period.
items.retired: Method name describes the answer (point-to-point = two points).

facts.statement: Indexed annuity contracts commonly let the insurer change features like the cap periodically.
facts.quote: Indexed annuity contracts commonly allow the insurance company to change some of these features periodically, such as the rate cap.

items.stem: A client bought an indexed annuity with a 7% cap. Two years later the cap for the new period is 5%. Is this typical?
options: No, a cap is locked in at issue for the whole contract
No, the participation rate may change but the cap may not
Yes, but a new cap has to be higher than the old one
Yes, insurers commonly reset caps from period to period
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor Bulletin: Indexed Annuities, indexed annuity contracts commonly allow the insurer to change some features periodically, such as the rate cap.

facts.statement: Once annuity income payments begin, the owner generally cannot withdraw money from the account.
facts.quote: annuities do not allow you to withdraw money from your account once you have started receiving income payments

items.stem: A retiree annuitized her variable annuity last year and now receives monthly income. She wants to take out a lump sum for a home repair. In general:
options: She can withdraw from the account at any time
She can withdraw up to 10% per year without penalty
She cannot withdraw from the account once payments have begun
She can withdraw after the surrender period ends
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor.gov: Variable Annuities, annuities generally do not allow withdrawals from the account once income payments have started.

facts.statement: A common variable annuity death benefit pays the greater of the account value or a guaranteed minimum such as purchase payments minus withdrawals.
facts.quote: your beneficiary may receive the greater of: (i) all the money in your account; or (ii) some guaranteed minimum, such as all purchase payments minus prior withdrawals

items.stem: A variable annuity owner paid in $100,000, took no withdrawals, and dies during the accumulation phase when the account is worth $82,000. The contract has a common standard death benefit. The beneficiary most likely receives:
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor.gov: Variable Annuities, a common death benefit pays the greater of the account value or a guaranteed minimum such as purchase payments minus prior withdrawals. The greater of $82,000 and $100,000 is $100,000.
